Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

abstract adjective

existing as an idea, not as a thing

also abstraction, in the abstract, abstract idea, not concrete, intangible

classical

Cic. Top. 26–27: earum rērum quae sunt … earum quae intelleguntur

quod intellegitur

phrase: a relative clause, in the number and gender of the thing meant (quae intelleguntur)

what is grasped by the mind (as against what can be seen and touched)

Classical Latin has no adjective for “abstract”. Cicero sets things that can be seen and touched (quae cernī tangīque possunt: a farm, a house, a wall) against things that cannot be touched or pointed to but are seen by the mind and understood (quae … cernī tamen animō atque intellegī possunt: guardianship, kinship), “under which there lies no body” (quārum rērum nūllum subest quasi corpus, Top. 27). Say so with a relative clause.

Other words

  • abstractus, abstracta, abstractum — abstract (as against concrete)

    declension · also used · late Latin · Isid. Orig. 2.24.14: quantitās abstracta (Lewis & Short, s.v. abstrahō); M-O s.v. abstract

    The word of the later philosophers and grammarians, and of the modern languages; classically only the participle of abstrahō, “dragged away”.

Examples

  • Nōn esse rūrsus ea dīcō quae tangī dēmōnstrārīve nōn possunt, cernī tamen animō atque intellegī possunt

    Those things, on the other hand, I call non-existent which cannot be touched or pointed out, but can still be seen by the mind and understoodCic. Top. 27

See also theory, idea.

SourcesLewis & Short: abstraho · Lewis & Short: intellego

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. abstract.
